name: System justification
statement: People are motivated to defend and rationalise the social, economic and political arrangements they live under, sometimes against their own interests.
meaning: Three claims travel under one name and only two have been tested at scale. The first is that a system-justifying motive exists alongside motives to defend the self and the ingroup. That is a framework rather than a prediction, and it is compatible with almost any pattern of results. The second is the status-legitimacy hypothesis: that people disadvantaged by a hierarchy legitimise it more than the advantaged do, because the clash between their position and their belief in the system produces dissonance they resolve in the system's favour. That claim is sharp, it is falsifiable, and most of the argument about system justification theory has been about it. The third is the palliative function: that holding system-justifying beliefs makes people feel better, which is why they hold them. The verdict below is about the second claim and about the experimental literature that grew around the first.

origin.who: John T. Jost and Mahzarin R. Banaji
origin.note: Their paper is "The role of stereotyping in system-justification and the production of false consciousness", in a special issue on social stereotyping. Jost's 2019 retrospective in the same journal says the aim was to explain 'the participation by disadvantaged individuals and groups in negative stereotypes of themselves' and the related phenomenon of outgroup favouritism. The term itself came from a line in Kluegel and Smith's 1986 book. The 1994 paper made no status-legitimacy prediction. That came nine years later, in Jost, Pelham, Sheldon and Ni Sullivan's survey paper. The 1994 text was not retrieved for this entry, and the account of it here is Jost's own from 2019.

evidence: The status-legitimacy hypothesis was set out by Jost, Pelham, Sheldon and Ni Sullivan across five US national survey studies, published in the European Journal of Social Psychology in 2003. Their abstract reports six results. Low-income respondents and African Americans were more likely than others to support limits on the right of citizens and the media to criticise the government. Low-income Latinos trusted US government officials more, and were more likely to say the government is run for the benefit of all, than high-income Latinos. Low-income respondents were more likely to say large pay differences are needed to motivate effort. Southerners endorsed meritocratic belief systems more than Northerners, and poor Southern African Americans more than affluent Northern ones. Low-income respondents and African Americans were more likely to call economic inequality legitimate and necessary. Stronger meritocratic belief went with greater satisfaction with one's own economic situation. The paper's full text was not retrieved for this entry, so no coefficient from it is quoted here. The experimental branch of the literature ran separately, using manipulations meant to raise system-justifying motivation, including system threat, system dependence, complementary stereotypes and meritocracy primes.

replication.headline: In 66 samples across 30 countries, higher subjective status went with seeing the system as more legitimate, and the association was positive in every country.
replication.detail: Brandt and 65 co-authors collected 12,788 responses in 66 samples across 30 countries and regressed four measures of perceived legitimacy on country-mean-centred subjective status. The slope was b = 0.152, SE 0.005, 95% CI [0.142, 0.162], which they describe as a 15% difference in perceived legitimacy between the highest and lowest levels of subjective status. Adding age, gender, sample type and measure type left it at b = 0.151, SE 0.005, 95% CI [0.141, 0.161]. With random slopes by country the estimate stayed positive in every country. Eight moderators were tested, and at no level of any of them did the association turn negative. Their power analysis put detection of a slope of 0.02 at about 49%. The earlier large-sample test points the same way. Brandt pooled the American National Election Studies, the General Social Survey and the World Values Survey, 151,794 respondents in total. His abstract reports that the average effect across years and countries 'was most often directly contrary to the status-legitimacy hypothesis or was practically zero'. The two moderators he tested, inequality and civil liberties, gave weak, null or contrary evidence. Valdes, Liu and Williams tried to repeat Li and colleagues' Chinese finding in stratified quota samples of 1,004 people in China and 1,161 in the United States, measured twice six months apart. Subjective status correlated positively with system justification in both, r = .31 in China and r = .30 in the United States, and held cross-lagged. The objective-status result that had supported the hypothesis did not repeat. The experimental literature has its own problem. Sotola and Credé ran a z-curve over 116 papers and 232 samples, entering 180 significant p-values. They estimated an expected replication rate of .18, 98% CI [.10, .30], against an observed discovery rate of .78 and an expected discovery rate of .14. Studies using system-threat manipulations came out worst, with an expected replication rate of .11 and a Sorić false discovery rate of .66. One of these experiments has been tested directly. Caruso, Vohs, Baxter and Waytz reported that showing people a faint image of banknotes raised system justification at d = 0.80, 95% CI [0.05, 1.54]. Many Labs 1 repeated it in 36 samples with 6,333 participants and found a weighted d of -0.02, 99% CI [-0.08, 0.04], with 97% of samples returning nothing and the aggregate test at t(6331) = -0.79, p = .83.

study.cite: Brandt, M. J., Kuppens, T., Spears, R., et al. (2020). Subjective status and perceived legitimacy across countries. European Journal of Social Psychology, 50(5), 921-942.

replicated.unit: share of the perceived-legitimacy scale, across the full range of subjective status
replicated.weighting: multilevel, measures nested in persons in samples in countries

limits: Support for the status-legitimacy hypothesis exists and is narrow. Sengupta, Osborne and Sibley found it in a New Zealand probability sample of 6,162 people, but only on one of two measures. Asians rated ethnic-group relations fairer than Europeans did, Cohen's d = -.32 for the European-Asian gap, and Pacific Islanders more so still, d = -.36. On general support for the political system there was no gap between Europeans, Asians and Pacific people, and Māori, the group with the most politicised identity, scored lowest of all, d = -.37 against Europeans. Henry and Saul's Bolivian study and Li and colleagues' Chinese study are cited on the supportive side by both camps; neither was retrieved for this entry. The palliative function is a separate question with its own evidence. Vargas-Salfate, Paez, Khan, Liu and Gil de Zúñiga ran a two-wave longitudinal survey of representative online samples in 18 countries, N = 5,901. They report that system justification was positively related to life satisfaction and negatively to anxiety and depression. Neither country-level inequality nor individual social status changed the relationship. Their coefficients were not retrieved, so none appears here. The same group's 19-nation comparison of social dominance theory and system justification, which Brandt and colleagues list among the studies finding no support for the status-legitimacy hypothesis, is behind a paywall and its numbers are not quoted here. Brandt's 2013 full text was also not obtained, and the figures above from it come from its own abstract. Jost's 2020 book, published by Harvard University Press, was not read for this entry. A z-curve is a forecast of how often significant findings would repeat, not a demonstration that any particular one is false, and Sotola and Credé's post-2015 subset came out better than the pre-2015 one on every index they report.
misreadings: The most common error is treating a failed status-legitimacy hypothesis as a refutation of system justification theory. Jost rejects the equation, and in print. He writes that his group 'never regarded dissonance reduction as the "engine" of system justification'. Brandt, he says, 'went so far as to rename the strong, dissonance-based hypothesis the "status-legitimacy hypothesis"' and extended it to gender and education, which were not part of the original programme. He also quotes his own 2003 paper as having said that disadvantaged groups are not 'always (or even ordinarily) the most likely ones to provide ideological support for the system'. His question is a different one: why do members of the working class defend the status quo as much as they do, rather than more than the rich do. The second error runs the other way. Brandt's null results also gave little support to group self-interest, so they do not vindicate social identity or realistic conflict accounts by default. Jost makes that point, and Brandt's own later work finds a positive slope rather than the flat one. The third is to read the theory's supportive correlational literature as evidence for the causal story. People with lower subjective status report lower perceived legitimacy, which is what self-interest predicts and what the theory's sharp prediction denies.
